Comments 1.4 Fire Department Notification and Emergency Procedures 1.4.1 Fire Department notification for impairment It is important that the department be notified if a standpipe system, sprinkler system or fire alarm system is out of service, whether because of a planned removal from service or an unplanned out-of-service condition. (1) Standpipe systems. Notification must be made to the department whenever a standpipe system is or will be out of service for any period of time. (2) Sprinkler systems and fire alarm systems. Notification that a sprinkler system or fire alarm system, or any part, is or will be out of service must be made to the department under the following circumstances: • The sprinkler system or fire alarm system is or will be out of service on more than one floor of a building; or • With respect to a sprinkler system, the work or repairs cannot be completed, and the system restored to service, within 8 hours of the time the system was placed or went out of service; or • With respect to a fire alarm system, the work or repairs will require the fire alarm system to be out of service for more than 8 hours in any 24-hour period; or • One or more other fire protection systems in the area in which a fire protection system is out of service are or will also be out of service at the same time. The general information (non-emergency) numbers that should be used for notifications are: Manhattan Brooklyn Queens Bronx Staten Island (212) 570-4300 (718) 965-8300 (718) 476-6200 (718) 430-0200 (718) 494-4296 The impairment coordinator must be able to give the following information: • The building owner’s or impairment coordinator’s name and contact information; • the building address; • the type of fire protection system that is out of service; • whether the out-of-service is planned or unplanned; • if a planned removal from service, the date and time the fire protection system will be placed out of service, and the estimated duration the system will be out of service; • If an unplanned out-of-service condition, the estimated duration the system will be out of service; • The floors or areas in which the fire protection system is out of service; • if the other fire protection systems are in good working order; • The name and certificate number of the Certificate of Fitness holder responsible for supervision of the fire protection system that is out of service. 1.4.2 Emergency notification and procedures Fire guards must have a method of contacting emergency services. Fire guards can use cell phones to make notifications. They must ensure that there is enough battery power to cover their shift. Notifying by phone is the most direct and effective way to notify the Fire Department. If a fire guard becomes aware of a fire, he/she must immediately call 911 and report the emergency. There must be no delays in making a notification. The Fire Department can also be notified using a street fire alarm pull station. The fire guard must also sound the fire alarm pull station (where available) to alert the occupants. The fire guard must also immediately notify the impairment coordinator, FLSD, CSFSM or other on-site responsible personnel, but only after calling 911. The responsible person will give directions to the fire guard. The fire guard must follow those instructions. For example, the FLSD may inform the fire guard of the safest evacuation route from the building. When notifying 911 of a fire or other emergency, the call-taker will need to know certain information about the emergency. Obviously, the nature of the emergency and address are the most critical pieces of information. The operator may also ask what the nearest crossstreet is, and if anyone needs medical attention and if so, what their symptoms are. Additionally, if you are responsible for a very large construction site or large building, it is likely that there will be more than one means of entry. It would be helpful to provide information on which entrance offers the quickest access to the emergency area, so emergency responders can reach it faster. If certain entrances are obstructed and are not easily accessible by emergency responders, this information must be communicated to the 911 operator. The more information you have available to communicate with the 911 operator, the easier it will be to get the right kind of help, quickly. When you call 911, in addition to the information mentioned above, you should be prepared to answer other questions, which may include: • The phone number you are calling from • The nature of the emergency • Details about the emergency, such as a description of any fire that may be burning, or a description of injuries or symptoms being experienced by the person having a medical emergency. Be prepared to follow any instructions the operator gives you. Many 911 operators can tell you exactly what to do to help, while waiting for emergency services to arrive. Finally, do not hang up the phone until the operator instructs you to. In case of a fire emergency, occupants may have to be evacuated. Occupants on the fire floor and the floor above are in the greatest danger and must be evacuated first. The fire guard responsible for helping with the evacuation should be calm and in control of the situation. Fire guards need to speak in a clear manner while helping with the evacuation. Their instructions and actions play an important role in controlling panic in an emergency. Occupants should be told to be calm and move quickly to the closest exit. The fire guard should tell the occupants to avoid the elevators and direct them to use stairwells to exit. After the FDNY arrives, the fire guard should be sure to meet the emergency responders to provide them with information regarding the nature of the emergency, its location and to provide the information that the emergency responders request. 1.4.3 Manual or pull station devices The purpose of a fire alarm system is to warn the occupants to leave the premises in case of a fire or other emergency. Some fire alarm systems are activated automatically. Other must be activated manually. Fire alarm systems that are manually activated use fire alarm pull stations. The manual pull stations may not directly transmit a signal to the FDNY. A phone call must always be made to 911 or the FDNY dispatcher. DONT assume that the FDNY has been called if you hear a fire alarm or smoke detector sound. Fire alarm pull stations are located near the exits in the protected area, they must be visible, clear, and reachable. There must be at least 1 manual fire alarm station on each floor of a building (except residential buildings). Manual fire alarm pull stations should be of opposite color to the background on which they installed on. Approved plastic covers may be used to protect fire alarm pull stations. They help to avoid false alarms. There are 2 types of manual fire alarm pull stations, single action and double action. A. Single action stations: Single action stations take only 1 step to sound the alarm. The cover on these alarm stations serves as a lever. This kind of alarm station is often found indoors, e.g., in office buildings. When the cover is pulled down, it sends the alarm signal. Single action stations Activating a single action station B. Double action stations: Double action stations require 2 steps in order to activate the alarm. The user must: • Break a glass, open a door or lift a cover, • Then gain access to a switch or lever which must then be operated to initiate an alarm. To activate this type of alarm station the cover must be lifted before the lever is pulled. This kind of double action station is often found indoors. Another kind of double action break glass station requires someone to break a small glass with a small metal mallet. Double action station Activate a double action station The fire guard must know how to manually work each alarm station on his site. Once activated, the fire alarm system cannot be reset at the fire alarm manual pull station. The alarm must be reset at the main FACP (Fire Alarm Control Panel). The alarm may be reset only by an S-95 Certificate of Fitness holder after being advised by a Fire Department representative. Once alarm is activated, a key may be needed to reset the manual pull station. Fire guards should be familiar with the location of all fire protection devices and fire alarm pull stations. The handle should be at least 4 feet from the floor. Pull stations must be located within 5 feet from the exit doorway opening and never be blocked. 1.4.4 Safety requirements Several types of safety signs may be posted at different locations inside the building. example, these signs may be: For (a) The general behavior is to be followed during a fire emergency. (b) The location of fire extinguishers and emergency exits. (c) How to use the fire extinguishers and related emergency equipment. (d) How to sound the fire alarm in case of an emergency. (e) Banned use of elevators during fire emergencies unless instructed by the Fire Department. (f) The floor numbers. The fire guard should be aware of the fire safety sign requirements. Being aware of the signs help fire guard perform his work. He/she should also make sure that exit signs posted above doors are always lit (illuminated). Examples of these signs are shown on the next page. Typical Safety Signs Exit Signs Special Exit Signs Fire Extinguisher Sign Sprinkler Sign Elevator Warning Sign No-smoking Sign Stair Signs (posted by outside of door) (posted by door inside of stairwell) PART 2. FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM AND FIRE EXTINGUISHERS 2.1 Sprinkler System A sprinkler system is required by FDNY rules. As required by law, all apartment buildings built after March 1999 need to have fire sprinkler systems installed. Fire sprinklers consist of a water supply system that delivers suitable pressure and flows to a water distribution piping system, connected to fire sprinklers. The purpose of sprinklers is to control and possibly extinguish the fire. Sprinklers are intended to control the heat release rate of the fire. Sprinklers can cool the nearby items to prevent the spread of fire. When sprinklers are out of service or not installed, the chances property loss because of a fire will increase. **It is important to know about materials that are stored in the building as water reactive materials may present special risks in an area. The sprinkler system has automatic devices made to release water on a fire. These devices are called sprinkler heads. The sprinkler heads are usually covered by a disk or cap. This cap is held in place by a heat sensitive releasing part. A rise in temperature to a preset level causes the sprinkler head to open. Water is then released in the form of spray. The term “fused” means that sprinkler heads opened. Sprinkler heads are installed at regular intervals on the piping. If more than one head opens, the area is sprayed by each sprinkler head, and spray pattern may overlap. An S-12 COF holder (Supervision of Citywide Sprinkler System) is responsible for conducting inspections and certifying system compliance with the NYC Fire Code. A typical sprinkler head is shown in the picture below. A TYPICAL SPRINKLER HEAD 2.2 Standpipe System A standpipe system is the part of the fire protection system that is made to give fast access to water in the event of a fire. Standpipes are fitted as individual systems and act as a building’s fire hydrants. Standpipe systems can be added to sprinkler systems. Sprinklers may be automatic or manual as well as connection points for fire hoses. If the standpipe system is out-of-service, fire fighters may not have access to water delivery for manual firefighting. These systems are mostly installed in buildings which are tall, large, or highly specialized. Dry standpipe systems have a series of pipes which bring water to various points in a building. The pipes are dry and empty when not in use. Wet systems are “charged,” meaning that they are always filled with water. 2.3 Fire Alarm System Manual fire alarm pull station Smoke detector Fire alarm systems are required in many buildings as part of the fire protection system. A fire alarm system consists of parts arranged to detect and alarm the status of signalinitiating devices. If threat is found, the system will provide the correct response to the signal. In general, a fire alarm system may be automatic, manually activated, or both. If a fire occurs, the alarm system warns the tenants within the premises by triggering loud sirens, gongs, bells, speakers, horns and flashing lights. An S-95 Certificate of Fitness holder is responsible for performing inspections and ensuring the maintenance of Fire Alarm System. 2.4 Portable Fire Extinguishers The fire guard should know how to use the fire extinguisher and other basic firefighting equipment. In residential buildings, a portable fire extinguisher may not be available. The fire guard should know the type and size of fire extinguisher available/needed while performing the duty. All fire extinguishers must be mounted so that the top of the extinguisher is not more than 5 feet above the floor. The bottom of the fire extinguisher should be at least 4 inches from the floor. Fire extinguishers are NOT allowed to be on the floor. Correct installation Incorrect installation (1)The top of the fire extinguishers must not be more than 5 ft. above the floor. (2)The fire extinguishers must be accessible and unobstructed. The bottom of the extinguisher must be at least 4 in. above the floor. If the fire extinguisher has been used (discharged), a fully charged replacement is required before work can restart. Portable fire extinguishers are important in stopping a small fire from becoming a larger. Portable extinguishers are not intended to fight large or spreading fires. By the time the fire has spread, portable fire extinguishers will not be enough to kill the fire. Such fires should be extinguished by the building fire extinguishing systems or trained firefighters only. In case of any fire, 911 must be dialed. Fire extinguishers must be used in accordance with the rules printed on the side of the extinguisher. They plainly define how to use the extinguisher in case of an emergency. Fire Guards must know the different types of fire extinguishers available at the work site, which type to use, and how to use it correctly. Fire guards are responsible for extinguishing fires when they are small in size. The Fire Guard Certificate of Fitness holder should know how to use the portable fire extinguishers. When it comes to using a fire-extinguisher just remember P.A.S.S. P.A.S.S. stands for Pull, Aim, Squeeze, and Sweep. An example of instructions is shown below: Class A fires are caused by ordinary combustible materials (such as wood, paper, and cloth). To extinguish a Class A fire, extinguishers should utilize either the heat-absorbing effects of water or the coating effects of certain dry chemicals. Class B fires are caused by flammable or combustible liquids and gases such as oil, gasoline, etc. To extinguish a Class B fire, the blanketing-smothering effect of oxygen-excluding media such as CO2, dry chemical or foam is most effective. Class C fires involve electrical equipment. These fires must be fought with fire extinguishers that do not conduct electricity. Foam and water type extinguishers must not be used to extinguish electrical fires. After shutting off the electrical equipment, extinguishers for Class A or B fires may be used. Class D fires are caused by ignitable metals, such as magnesium, titanium, and metallic sodium, or metals that are combustible under certain conditions, such as calcium, zinc, and aluminum. Water should not be used to extinguish Class D fires. A multi-purpose dry chemical fire extinguisher may be used to extinguish more than 2 classes of fire. The symbols show the type of fire the extinguisher may be used on. Examples of these symbols are shown on the next page. The symbol with the shaded background and the slash indicates the extinguisher that must NOT be used. The Certificate of Fitness holder must know these symbols. All fire extinguishers should be always kept in good working order. Fire Extinguisher Identification Symbols 2.4.2 Portable Fire Extinguisher Tags Installed portable fire extinguishers must have an FDNY standard PFE tag affixed. This tag will have important information about the extinguisher. By November 15, 2019, all portable fire extinguishers must have the new PFE tags. The FDNY will only recognize new PFE tags and will be issuing violations to businesses that have PFE installed without a proper tag. The color of the fire extinguishers may be changed by the FDNY every few years. The FDNY recommends two ways to verify the tag’s legitimacy: 1. Hologram: A real hologram strip shown on the tag is 3 inches long by ¼ inch wide. Counterfeit tags will NOT have a high-quality silver hologram. The hologram on a counterfeit tag will NOT change color as it is moved against the light. 2. QR code IF you scan the QR code, it should direct you to the updated FDNY approved fire extinguisher company list. You could use the company list to verify if the company printed on the list is currently approved by the FDNY. If your PFE tags cannot be verified via these two methods, contact your supervisor. If you suspect your PFE is a counterfeit, contact FDNY immediately by e-mail: Tags.Decal@fdny.nyc.gov PFE tag (This tag was released for 2021-2023) Tag colors and year will change every few years for security purposes. 2.4.3 Fire extinguisher inspections MONTHLY The portable fire extinguishers are required to be checked monthly. The owner of the business is responsible for selecting a person to do a monthly inspection. This monthly inspection is called a "quick check". The QUICK CHECK must check if: (1) the fire extinguisher is fully charged; (2) it is in its designated place; (3) it has not been actuated or tampered with; (4) there is no obvious or physical damage or condition to prevent its operation. The information of the monthly inspection record must include the date of the inspection, the name/initials of the person who did the inspection. This monthly quick check record must be kept on the back of the PFE tag or by an approved electronic method that provides a permanent record. ANNUALLY At least annually all Portable Fire Extinguishers must be checked by a W-96 Certificate of Fitness holder from FDNY approved company. After each annual inspection W-96 COF holder will replace the PFE tag. The information on the annual inspection record must be indicated on the new PFE tag. PART 3: Lithium-Ion Battery Safety Lithium-ion safety Lithium-ion batteries are rechargeable batteries found in electric bikes, scooters, cars, laptops, tablets, phones, and many other common household devices. Lithium-ion battery fires have caused deaths, serious injuries, and devastating damage to property around the city. It’s important to follow rules for safe storage, charging, and disposal for these types of batteries. If you own a lithium-ion powered device or plan to buy one, the FDNY has important safety tips that you should follow. These tips apply to all devices powered by lithium-ion batteries, including phones, tablets, laptops, e-cigarettes, toys, high-tech luggage, and even robotic vacuum cleaners. Immediately stop using or charging battery and call 911 if you notice: • Fire or Smoke • Overheating • Change in color or shape • Odd noises • Leaking • Strange smell

Charging Lithium Ion Lithium-ion batteries do not have to be fully charged; partial charge is the most suitable. When charging more than five (5) personal mobility devices or their removable batteries, it must be in a dedicated room with ventilation and a self-closing door. For a total battery capacity of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh), a 2-foot separation between charging batteries is required. For a total battery capacity up to 50 kWh, a 3-foot separation is needed. Chargers must only be used with a compatible battery pack. The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) charger interplays with the battery pack using the battery management system (BMS). The wrong battery/charger combination may not work safely. For example, the 100% cutoff to prevent overcharging, which damages batteries, may not work, which can easily create hazardous conditions such as fires, explosions and/or injuries. Always check with the manufacturer or retailer of the personal mobility device, an authorized repair shop or a testing laboratory such as Underwrites Laboratories (UL) to see if replacement is recommended or listed and safe for use with that device. Using unauthorized parts, including batteries and/or chargers, may cause damage, fire and possibly void your warranty. Extinguishing Lithium-ion Water may not prevent a battery from burning and spreading. Battery cells are known to explode and quickly spread to another battery. It can spread to another devices. Fire Extinguishers do not work on lithium-ion batteries fires. Unexpected Re-ignition. Reignition is common. Lithium-Ion Batteries are known to unexpectedly re-ignite (without warning) minutes, hours and even days after all visible fire has been put out. Lithium-ion batteries can enter an uncontrollable, self-heating state. This can result in the release of gas, cause fire and possible explosions. These batteries may continue to generate heat even when there is no visible sign of fire. Once heat reaches a certain level, fire may reignite on the battery and surrounding area. fdny.exp: Emergency Preparedness Plan: Emergency preparedness plans ensure that, in the event of a fire or a non-fire emergency, there are procedures in place that can be timely implemented to provide the information, guidance, direction and assistance needed to protect the safety of building occupants, including, if necessary, effecting their evacuation, relocation or sheltering in place. Such emergency preparedness plans assures that knowledgeable assistance is readily available on the premises to emergency response personnel responding to a fire or non-fire emergency at the premises. The emergency preparedness plan is also known as the fire safety and evacuation plan and/or emergency action plan.

fdny.exp: Impairment: Any condition in which a fire protection system cannot perform its designed fire safety function. Fire protection systems include sprinkler systems, standpipe systems and fire alarm systems. Examples of an impaired sprinkler or standpipe system may include an out-of-service fire pump. An example of an out-of service fire alarm system may include a shutdown of a floor’s fire alarm system detecting devices (to prevent an unnecessary alarm) while torch work associated with construction work is conducted.

fdny.exp: Two-Way Voice Communication: a form of transmission in which both parties involved can transmit information. This is useful during an emergency and allows staff members to report the conditions of a fire emergency from the fire floor back to the Fire and Life Safety Director or Coordinator of Fire Safety & Alarm Systems in Homeless Shelters or Fire and Emergency Drill Conductor in the lobby at the fire command center. Two-way voice communication uses warden phones that are placed at several locations throughout the building, usually near the exit stairways in the building.

fdny.exp: Free Burning Stage of a Fire: The fully developed stage of a fire. This is the second stage of the three stages of a fire. Generally during this stage the entire room and all of its contents are burning. The fire is still fuel regulated but is rapidly consuming the available fuel. If no efforts are made to extinguish the fire, it will continue to burn until the available fuel and/or oxygen in the area or room has been consumed.

cna.q: A nurse aide observes a resident has bruising on both arms. What is the FIRST action to take?
choices: Document it in the chart and say nothing
Report the observation immediately to the licensed nurse
Confront the aide who was on the previous shift
Wait to see if more bruising appears before reporting
cna.exp: Nurse aides have a legal obligation to immediately report observations of possible abuse or injury to the supervising licensed nurse. Documentation follows — reporting comes first.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: What is the correct order in the chain of command for a nurse aide?
choices: Nurse aide → doctor → administrator
Nurse aide → licensed nurse → charge nurse
Nurse aide → family member → licensed nurse
Nurse aide → other aides → director of nursing
cna.exp: Nurse aides report directly to the licensed nurse (LPN or RN). The chain is: nurse aide → licensed nurse → charge nurse → supervisor. Never skip a level.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: A resident tells a nurse aide, 'I don't want my daughter to know about my health.' The aide should:
choices: Tell the daughter anyway because family has the right to know
Respect the resident's wish — this is protected by HIPAA
Inform the charge nurse that the resident is difficult
Document that the resident is confused
cna.exp: HIPAA protects the resident's right to confidentiality. Residents have the right to control who receives their health information, including family members.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: Which behavior by a nurse aide is an example of resident abuse?
choices: Repositioning a resident every 2 hours
Calling a resident 'sweetie' instead of their name
Withholding a resident's meal because they were uncooperative
Documenting a resident's refusal of medication
cna.exp: Withholding food as punishment is a form of physical abuse and neglect. Using nicknames may be inappropriate but is not abuse; the other options are proper care.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: When documenting care, a nurse aide should ALWAYS:
choices: Write in pencil so corrections can be made easily
Sign with initials only to save time
Record only unusual events — skip routine care
Record accurately and completely, then sign with full name/title
cna.exp: Documentation must be accurate, complete, legible, and signed with the nurse aide's full name and title. Pencil is not acceptable; routine care must be documented.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: A nurse aide uses proper body mechanics. This means the aide should:
choices: Bend at the waist to lift a resident
Keep feet together to maintain balance
Bend at the knees and keep the back straight when lifting
Twist the body when transferring a resident
cna.exp: Proper body mechanics: bend knees (not waist), keep back straight, keep load close to body, and avoid twisting. This prevents musculoskeletal injury to both aide and resident.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: A resident's family member demands to see the resident's medical chart. The nurse aide should:
choices: Show them the chart — they have the right as family
Refuse and explain only the nurse or doctor can authorize access
Hand them the chart to avoid conflict
Make a copy of the chart for the family
cna.exp: Medical records are confidential. Only the resident or designated authorized persons may access medical records. The aide should direct the family to the charge nurse.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: The Nurse Aide Registry is:
choices: A list of all medications a nurse aide can administer
A state-maintained record of certified nurse aides, including abuse findings
A log of every resident a nurse aide has cared for
A schedule of continuing education requirements
cna.exp: States maintain a Nurse Aide Registry (NAR) listing all certified CNAs and any substantiated findings of abuse, neglect, or misappropriation of property.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: Which action by a nurse aide BEST promotes resident self-determination?
choices: Choosing the resident's clothing to save time
Asking the resident what they want to wear that day
Telling the resident what they will eat at each meal
Bathing the resident at the facility's convenience
cna.exp: Self-determination means residents have the right to make their own choices. Asking about clothing preferences respects autonomy and dignity.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: A nurse aide disagrees with a care decision. The BEST response is to:
choices: Refuse to carry out the care plan
Ignore the plan and do what seems best
Express concerns to the charge nurse through proper channels
Complain to other nurse aides
cna.exp: Concerns should be communicated professionally through the chain of command. Refusing care or changing the care plan without authorization is inappropriate.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: A nurse aide finds a resident's dentures on the floor. The aide should:
choices: Throw them away if broken
Clean them, label them, and report to the nurse
Give them to the roommate to hold
Leave them on the bedside table without reporting
cna.exp: Residents' personal property must be protected and cared for. The aide should clean the dentures, ensure they're labeled, and report the incident to the nurse.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Role of the Nurse Aide

cna.q: A nurse aide enters a resident's room and smells smoke. The FIRST action is to:
choices: Open the window to clear the air
Pull the fire alarm and call for help immediately
Look for the source of the smoke before alerting anyone
Continue with the scheduled care
cna.exp: RACE: Rescue → Alarm → Confine → Extinguish. The first priority after removing residents in immediate danger is activating the fire alarm.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: A resident tells the nurse aide they feel dizzy when standing up. This is called:
choices: Hypertension
Orthostatic hypotension
Bradycardia
Hypoglycemia
cna.exp: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension is a drop in blood pressure when changing from lying/sitting to standing. Residents should be helped to sit at the edge of the bed before standing.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: Which measure BEST prevents falls for a resident who is unsteady?
choices: Applying a full-body physical restraint
Placing a call light within reach and answering call lights promptly
Putting side rails up on all four sides of the bed
Leaving the resident alone to build confidence
cna.exp: Fall prevention focuses on accessibility, monitoring, and environment. Call light availability and prompt response are key. Restraints require physician orders and carry significant risks.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: A nursing home uses physical restraints. Nurse aides should know that restrained residents must be:
choices: Restrained for no more than 2 hours without being released
Released, repositioned, and toileted at least every 2 hours
Left in restraints all night for safety
Only released by a nurse, not a nurse aide
cna.exp: CMS regulations require restrained residents be released at least every 2 hours for repositioning, exercise, toileting, and circulation checks.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: An ambulatory resident starts to fall while walking. The nurse aide should:
choices: Let the resident fall — it's safer than catching them
Grab the resident's arm and pull them upright
Lower the resident to the floor gently, protecting their head
Yell loudly to startle the resident upright
cna.exp: If a resident begins to fall, guide them down gently to protect from injury. Do not try to hold them upright — this can injure both resident and aide. Protect the head.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: The safest way to identify a resident before providing care is to:
choices: Ask the resident their name
Check the name on the door of their room
Check the resident's ID bracelet and/or photo ID per facility policy
Ask a family member who is visiting
cna.exp: Resident identification must use at least one facility-approved method — typically ID bracelet and/or photo. Asking the name alone is not reliable for confused residents.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: A nurse aide notices a wet floor near the bathroom. The BEST action is:
choices: Walk around it and continue with care
Clean it up immediately or place a wet floor sign and alert housekeeping
Report it in the next shift change
Tell the resident to be careful
cna.exp: Wet floors are an immediate fall hazard. The nurse aide should clean the spill immediately or mark it and alert housekeeping — never ignore or just warn others.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: Which is an example of a restraint alternative?
choices: Wrist restraints to prevent IV removal
Vest (Posey) restraints at night
Bed/chair alarms and increased supervision
Tying the resident loosely to the wheelchair
cna.exp: Restraint alternatives include bed/chair alarms, increased monitoring, positioning devices, and activities. These are preferred before considering physical restraints.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Promotion of Safety

cna.q: A resident is on a dysphagia diet. This means the resident:
choices: Cannot eat any solid food — liquids only
Has difficulty swallowing and needs food and/or liquids modified in texture
Is on a low-sodium diet for heart health
Is diabetic and needs carbohydrate counting
cna.exp: Dysphagia is difficulty swallowing. Dysphagia diets modify food texture and liquid thickness to reduce the risk of aspiration (food entering the airway).

cna.q: Active range of motion (ROM) exercises are performed:
choices: By the nurse aide moving the resident's joints
By the resident themselves, with or without guidance
Only by a physical therapist
While the resident is sleeping
cna.exp: Active ROM: the resident moves the joints themselves. Passive ROM: the aide moves the joints. Active-assistive ROM: the resident moves with some help. Active ROM builds strength.

cna.q: A resident is incontinent. The nurse aide should:
choices: Scold the resident to encourage control
Change the resident promptly and provide perineal care to prevent skin breakdown
Limit fluids so incontinence occurs less often
Leave the resident in wet clothing during the night shift
cna.exp: Prompt cleaning and perineal care after incontinence prevents skin breakdown and pressure injuries. Limiting fluids can cause dehydration and urinary tract infections.

cna.q: A pressure injury (pressure ulcer) is MOST likely to develop over:
choices: Abdominal tissue
Bony prominences such as the heels, sacrum, and hips
Soft tissue in the upper arms
The forehead
cna.exp: Pressure injuries develop when tissue is compressed between a bony prominence and an external surface. Common sites: sacrum, heels, hips, elbows, and back of head.

cna.q: How often should a bedbound resident be repositioned to prevent pressure injuries?
choices: Once per shift (every 8 hours)
Every 4 hours
At least every 2 hours
Only when the resident requests it
cna.exp: Standard practice is to reposition bedbound residents at least every 2 hours to relieve pressure and maintain skin integrity. More frequent repositioning may be ordered.

cna.q: A resident refuses a bath. The nurse aide should:
choices: Force the bath — hygiene is medically necessary
Report the refusal to the licensed nurse and document it
Skip the bath and not document it
Call the family to convince the resident
cna.exp: Residents have the right to refuse care. The aide must respect the refusal, report it to the licensed nurse, and document it. Never force care.

cna.q: When providing mouth care to an unconscious resident, the nurse aide should position the resident:
choices: Flat on their back (supine)
On their side with head slightly down
Sitting upright at 90 degrees
With the head elevated on two pillows
cna.exp: An unconscious resident cannot swallow or cough protectively. Side-lying with head slightly down prevents aspiration of fluids during oral care.

cna.q: A resident's weight has decreased 3 lbs in one week. The nurse aide should:
choices: Encourage extra snacks without reporting
Report this to the licensed nurse immediately
Ignore it — weight naturally fluctuates
Document it and wait 2 weeks to see if the trend continues
cna.exp: Unexplained or rapid weight loss is a significant clinical finding. Even a small loss over a short period should be reported promptly to the licensed nurse.

cna.q: Which observation about a resident's urine should be reported IMMEDIATELY?
choices: Urine that is pale yellow
Urine that is dark brown with a strong odor
Urine output of 400 mL over 8 hours
A resident voiding 5 times during a shift
cna.exp: Dark brown urine with strong odor can indicate dehydration, urinary tract infection, or kidney problems. This is an abnormal finding requiring immediate reporting.

cna.q: The purpose of an indwelling urinary catheter care is to:
choices: Increase urine output
Prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI)
Make repositioning easier
Replace the need for incontinence care
cna.exp: Catheter care (perineal cleaning around the catheter) prevents bacteria from entering the urinary tract and causing CAUTI, one of the most common healthcare-associated infections.

cna.q: A resident with a feeding tube begins coughing and appears to be choking during a tube feeding. The nurse aide should:
choices: Increase the feeding rate to push through the problem
Stop the feeding immediately and call for the nurse
Tilt the head back to open the airway
Turn the resident to the left side and continue feeding
cna.exp: Coughing during tube feeding suggests the feeding may be entering the airway (aspiration). Stop immediately and get the nurse — this is a medical emergency.

cna.q: A resident with dementia becomes agitated during a bath. The BEST response is to:
choices: Physically restrain the resident to complete the bath quickly
Stop the bath, allow the resident to calm down, and try again later
Raise your voice so the resident understands
Ignore the agitation and continue bathing
cna.exp: For cognitively impaired residents, reducing stress is key. Pausing an activity to allow the resident to calm down is therapeutic. Forcing care increases agitation and risk of injury.

cna.q: When communicating with a resident who has moderate dementia, the nurse aide should:
choices: Use complex sentences to stimulate cognitive function
Speak quickly to keep the resident's attention
Use simple, short sentences and maintain eye contact
Discuss the resident's condition with other aides in the room
cna.exp: Effective communication with cognitively impaired residents: short sentences, simple words, calm tone, eye contact, and non-verbal cues. Avoid correcting or arguing.

cna.q: A resident with Alzheimer's disease repeatedly asks where her husband is. He passed away 5 years ago. The BEST response is:
choices: Firmly remind her that her husband is dead each time
Tell her he just stepped out for a minute
Acknowledge her feelings: 'You're missing him. Let's look at some photos together.'
Ignore the question to avoid distressing her
cna.exp: Validation therapy focuses on acknowledging the feeling behind the question rather than correcting reality. Repeated correction causes distress without therapeutic benefit.

cna.q: Sundowning in dementia refers to:
choices: A morning confusion state
Increased confusion, agitation, and restlessness in late afternoon/evening
Sleep-wake cycle reversal where the resident sleeps all day
Depression triggered by reduced sunlight in winter
cna.exp: Sundowning is a pattern of increased confusion, agitation, and behavioral changes that typically occur in the late afternoon or evening in residents with dementia.

cna.q: A nurse aide is caring for a resident with dementia who is wandering. The BEST safety measure is:
choices: Locking the resident in their room
Using wander guard/elopement alarm systems and monitoring
Sedating the resident to prevent wandering
Applying wrist restraints when the aide is busy
cna.exp: Wander guard systems (door alarms, GPS bracelets) and supervision are the safest approach. Locking a resident in their room or using restraints is inappropriate.

cna.q: The MOST important action a nurse aide can take to prevent the spread of infection is:
choices: Wearing gloves for all resident contact
Washing hands before and after every resident contact
Wearing a mask during all care activities
Keeping resident rooms clean at all times
cna.exp: Hand hygiene is the single most effective method of preventing infection transmission. Gloves do not replace handwashing — hands must be washed before and after glove use.

cna.q: Standard precautions should be used:
choices: Only for residents known to have HIV or hepatitis
For residents on isolation precautions only
With all residents, for all care, at all times
Only when blood or body fluids are visible
cna.exp: Standard precautions apply to all patients at all times, regardless of diagnosis. They treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious.

cna.q: A nurse aide has just removed gloves after emptying a urinary catheter bag. The aide should:
choices: Put on a fresh pair of gloves immediately
Wash hands with soap and water or use hand sanitizer
Wipe hands on a paper towel — gloves protect enough
Proceed to the next resident — gloves were just removed
cna.exp: Gloves must be removed and hands must be cleaned after every resident contact or procedure. Gloves are contaminated after use and cannot substitute for hand hygiene.

cna.q: A resident has C. difficile (C. diff) diarrhea. Which precautions are required?
choices: Airborne precautions — negative pressure room
Droplet precautions — surgical mask required
Contact precautions — gown and gloves, and soap-and-water handwashing (not alcohol gel)
Standard precautions only
cna.exp: C. diff requires contact precautions. Critically: alcohol-based hand sanitizers do NOT kill C. diff spores. Soap-and-water handwashing is mandatory for C. diff.

cna.q: How should a nurse aide handle soiled linen?
choices: Shake the linen to air it out before placing in the hamper
Carry soiled linen close to the body to prevent dropping it
Hold away from body and place directly in the appropriate linen bag without shaking
Take soiled linen from room to room to save trips
cna.exp: Soiled linen must be handled minimally — never shaken (which spreads pathogens), held away from the uniform, and placed immediately in the correct linen bag.

cna.q: The correct order for donning (putting on) PPE is:
choices: Gloves → gown → mask → goggles
Gown → mask → goggles → gloves
Mask → gloves → gown → goggles
Goggles → gloves → mask → gown
cna.exp: CDC sequence for donning: Gown → Mask/respirator → Goggles/face shield → Gloves. The gown goes on first to protect clothing; gloves go on last to avoid contaminating them.

cna.q: A nurse aide accidentally sticks herself with a used needle. She should FIRST:
choices: Cover the wound with a bandage and continue working
Wash the area immediately with soap and water, then report to the supervisor
Apply hand sanitizer to the wound
Wait until the end of the shift to report it
cna.exp: Needlestick: immediately wash with soap and water, then report to the supervisor/occupational health. Prompt reporting allows evaluation of exposure risk and timely prophylaxis if needed.

cna.q: Which of the following is an example of medical asepsis?
choices: Using sterile gloves to change a wound dressing
Washing hands before preparing a meal tray
Wearing a sterile gown during surgery
Sterilizing instruments in an autoclave
cna.exp: Medical asepsis (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms. Handwashing is medical asepsis. Surgical asepsis (sterile technique) eliminates all microorganisms.

cna.q: A resident has tuberculosis (TB) and requires airborne precautions. The nurse aide should wear:
choices: Standard surgical mask
N95 respirator (fitted and tested)
Double-layered gloves
Gown and face shield only
cna.exp: Airborne precautions require an N95 respirator (not a surgical mask) because TB is transmitted by small airborne particles that can travel long distances. Fit testing is required.

cna.q: A nurse aide is taking a resident's oral temperature. The resident just drank hot coffee. The aide should:
choices: Take the temperature immediately — results are still accurate
Wait 15–20 minutes before taking the oral temperature
Use the armpit (axillary) instead — no wait time needed
Take a rectal temperature instead
cna.exp: Hot or cold foods/drinks alter oral temperature for 15–20 minutes. Wait before taking an oral temp to ensure accuracy, or use an alternate route.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A normal adult resting pulse rate is:
choices: 40–60 beats per minute
60–100 beats per minute
100–120 beats per minute
120–160 beats per minute
cna.exp: A normal adult resting heart rate is 60–100 bpm. Below 60 (bradycardia) or above 100 (tachycardia) should be reported to the nurse.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: When measuring blood pressure, the nurse aide should place the stethoscope over the:
choices: Radial artery at the wrist
Brachial artery in the antecubital space (inner elbow)
Femoral artery in the groin
Carotid artery in the neck
cna.exp: Blood pressure is measured using the brachial artery. The cuff is placed on the upper arm and the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the antecubital fossa.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A nurse aide is assigned to measure a resident's intake and output (I&O). Intake includes:
choices: Only IV fluids
All fluids taken by mouth and all IV/tube feeding fluids
Solid food only
Urine output minus the fluids consumed
cna.exp: Intake = all fluids entering the body: oral fluids, IV fluids, tube feedings, and irrigation fluids. Output = urine, liquid stool, wound drainage, and emesis.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A resident is described as being in the Fowler's position. This means the resident is:
choices: Lying flat on the back (supine)
Lying on the side
Semi-sitting with head elevated 45–60 degrees
Lying face down (prone)
cna.exp: Fowler's position: head of bed elevated 45–60 degrees. Semi-Fowler's is 30–45 degrees. Fowler's is used to improve breathing and reduce aspiration risk.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A resident's leg is edematous (swollen). When positioning this resident in bed, the nurse aide should:
choices: Keep the leg flat to avoid increasing pressure
Elevate the affected leg above the level of the heart
Place a heat pack on the leg
Position the resident on the affected side
cna.exp: Elevating an edematous extremity above heart level promotes venous and lymphatic drainage, reducing swelling through gravity.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A nurse aide notices a resident's surgical wound has increased redness, warmth, and yellowish drainage. The aide should:
choices: Change the dressing using clean technique
Report these signs of possible infection to the nurse immediately
Apply a warm compress to soothe the area
Document the observation and re-assess in 4 hours
cna.exp: Redness, warmth, swelling, and purulent (yellowish/greenish) drainage are signs of wound infection. This must be reported immediately — wound care decisions are made by the nurse/physician.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: The Heimlich maneuver is used when a person:
choices: Has a seizure
Has a complete airway obstruction and cannot speak or cough effectively
Is having a stroke
Has a nosebleed that won't stop
cna.exp: The Heimlich maneuver (abdominal thrusts) is used for a conscious adult with complete airway obstruction — they cannot speak, cough, or breathe effectively.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A nurse aide is caring for a resident who just had a seizure. AFTER the seizure ends, the aide should:
choices: Restrain the resident to prevent injury from a second seizure
Position the resident on their side (recovery position) and stay with them
Give the resident water to drink to prevent dehydration
Wake the resident immediately and help them walk
cna.exp: After a seizure: side-lying (recovery) position prevents aspiration, stay with the resident, do not restrain, assess for injury, and report to the nurse immediately.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A nurse aide is applying anti-embolic (TED) stockings. The stockings should be:
choices: Applied while the resident is sitting up after walking
Applied early in the morning before the resident gets out of bed
Worn only at night when the resident is sleeping
Applied only after the resident has been ambulating for 30 minutes
cna.exp: Anti-embolic stockings work best when applied before the resident gets up (when legs are less swollen from gravity). They prevent blood pooling and DVT in immobile residents.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A resident is on a 1500 mL fluid restriction per day. By 3 PM the resident has had 1200 mL. The nurse aide should:
choices: Give the resident no more fluids for the rest of the day
Report to the nurse — only 300 mL remains for the day
Encourage extra fluids since the resident looks thirsty
Give an additional 500 mL since the resident seems dehydrated
cna.exp: Fluid restrictions are physician orders. When approaching the limit, the nurse must be informed so care planning can be adjusted for the remaining fluid allocation.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A resident is receiving oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/min. The nurse aide should:
choices: Never change or adjust the flow rate without a nurse's order
Increase the rate if the resident says they feel short of breath
Remove it when the resident is eating
Store the oxygen tank horizontally to prevent falls
cna.exp: Oxygen flow rate is a physician order. The aide cannot adjust it. If the resident has difficulty breathing, call the nurse immediately. Oxygen tanks must be stored upright and secured.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: When providing pericare (perineal care) to a female resident, the nurse aide should cleanse:
choices: Back to front, using one stroke per wipe
Front to back, using one stroke per wipe
In a circular motion from outside to inside
From side to side across the entire perineum
cna.exp: Always cleanse female perineal area front to back (urethra to anus) to prevent fecal contamination of the urethra and vagina, which causes UTIs.
cna.source: CNA Certification Exam — Basic Nursing Care

cna.q: A nurse aide sees a resident who appears to be having a stroke — one side of their face is drooping and their arm is weak. The aide should:
choices: Give the resident aspirin and call family
Perform the Heimlich maneuver
Activate the emergency response immediately — do not leave the resident
Help the resident to bed and check vitals first
