choices: Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.
The absence of pathogens. 'Medical asepsis' (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms; 'surgical asepsis' (sterile technique) eliminates them entirely.
A microorganism (bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite) capable of causing disease.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — a dangerous antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Requires contact precautions (gown + gloves).
cna.exp: Droplet Precautions: Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.

cna.q: Which term means: “Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.”?
choices: Droplet Precautions
Contact Precautions
MRSA
Standard Precautions
cna.exp: Droplet Precautions: Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.

cna.q: What does “Airborne Precautions” mean?
choices: Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and negative-pressure room.
A microorganism (bacterium, virus, fungus, or parasite) capable of causing disease.
Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.
Specialized clothing or equipment worn by healthcare workers to protect against infection: gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, face shield.
cna.exp: Airborne Precautions: Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and negative-pressure room.

cna.q: Which term means: “Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and nega…”?
choices: Airborne Precautions
MRSA
Contact Precautions
Nosocomial Infection
cna.exp: Airborne Precautions: Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and negative-pressure room.

cna.q: What does “Asepsis” mean?
choices: A hospital-acquired infection — an infection a patient develops while receiving care that was not present on admission.
Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.
The absence of pathogens. 'Medical asepsis' (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms; 'surgical asepsis' (sterile technique) eliminates them entirely.
Specialized clothing or equipment worn by healthcare workers to protect against infection: gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, face shield.
cna.exp: Asepsis: The absence of pathogens. 'Medical asepsis' (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms; 'surgical asepsis' (sterile technique) eliminates them entirely.

cna.q: Which term means: “The absence of pathogens. 'Medical asepsis' (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms; 'surgical asepsis'…”?
choices: PPE (Personal Protective Equipment)
MRSA
Nosocomial Infection
Asepsis
cna.exp: Asepsis: The absence of pathogens. 'Medical asepsis' (clean technique) reduces the number of microorganisms; 'surgical asepsis' (sterile technique) eliminates them entirely.

cna.q: What does “Tachycardia” mean?
choices: High blood pressure — a reading consistently at or above 130/80 mmHg. A leading risk factor for stroke and heart disease.
The four primary measurements of body function: Temperature (T), Pulse (P), Respiration (R), Blood Pressure (BP). SpO₂ is often called the 5th vital sign.
Abnormally low blood pressure, generally below 90/60 mmHg. Can cause dizziness, fainting, or shock.
A heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute (bpm) at rest.
cna.exp: Tachycardia: A heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute (bpm) at rest.

cna.q: Which term means: “A heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute (bpm) at rest.”?
choices: Bradycardia
Tachycardia
Radial Pulse
Apical Pulse
cna.exp: Tachycardia: A heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute (bpm) at rest.

cna.q: What does “Fowler's Position” mean?
choices: A technique for turning a patient as a unit (head, spine, hips aligned) to protect the spine during repositioning. Requires two caregivers.
The full movement possible at a joint. ROM exercises maintain flexibility and prevent contractures. Active ROM: patient moves on their own. Passive ROM: CNA moves the li…
Patient lies flat on their back. Good for sleeping; increases pressure on the sacrum and heels — monitor for pressure ulcers.
A semi-upright position (45–60°) used to improve breathing, eat, and facilitate care. High Fowler's is 90°; Semi-Fowler's is 30–45°.
cna.exp: Fowler's Position: A semi-upright position (45–60°) used to improve breathing, eat, and facilitate care. High Fowler's is 90°; Semi-Fowler's is 30–45°.

cna.q: Which term means: “A semi-upright position (45–60°) used to improve breathing, eat, and facilitate care. High Fowler's is 90°; Semi-Fowler…”?
choices: Prone Position
Logrolling
Fowler's Position
Lateral (Side-Lying) Position
cna.exp: Fowler's Position: A semi-upright position (45–60°) used to improve breathing, eat, and facilitate care. High Fowler's is 90°; Semi-Fowler's is 30–45°.

cna.q: What does “Heimlich Maneuver” mean?
choices: The entry of food, liquid, saliva, or vomit into the lungs instead of the stomach — can cause aspiration pneumonia.
The skin's elasticity and ability to return to normal position after being pinched. Poor turgor (slow return, 'tenting') can indicate dehydration.
Infection control measures for pathogens spread by direct or indirect contact. Requires gloves and gown upon entering the room.
Abdominal thrusts used to dislodge an airway obstruction in a conscious adult who is choking.
cna.exp: Heimlich Maneuver: Abdominal thrusts used to dislodge an airway obstruction in a conscious adult who is choking.

cna.q: What does “Heimlich Maneuver” mean?
choices: Used for infections spread by respiratory droplets (>5 µm). Requires surgical mask when within 3 feet of the patient.
Abdominal thrusts used to dislodge an airway obstruction in a conscious adult who is choking.
The correct use of the body to prevent injury during lifting, moving, and transferring patients. Key principles: wide base of support, bend at knees, keep load close to…
A heart rate slower than 60 beats per minute at rest.
cna.exp: Heimlich Maneuver: Abdominal thrusts used to dislodge an airway obstruction in a conscious adult who is choking.

cna.q: What does “Recovery Position” mean?
choices: Intentional harm or mistreatment of a resident — physical, emotional, sexual, or financial. CNAs are MANDATORY REPORTERS and must report all suspected abuse immediately.
Information based on what the patient says or feels, not directly observable or measurable. Example: 'Patient states he has chest pain.'
A set of infection-control practices used with ALL patients regardless of diagnosis. Includes handwashing, gloves, masks, and safe handling of sharps.
An unconscious but breathing patient is placed on their side to prevent aspiration of vomit and maintain a clear airway.
cna.exp: Recovery Position: An unconscious but breathing patient is placed on their side to prevent aspiration of vomit and maintain a clear airway.

hha.q: Which of the following is WITHIN the scope of practice for a Home Health Aide (HHA)?
choices: Adjusting a client's insulin dose based on blood sugar readings
Assisting a client with bathing, dressing, and grooming
Changing a sterile wound dressing independently
Deciding to discontinue a prescribed medication
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: An HHA notices a significant change in a client's condition — the client is much more confused than usual. The HHA should:
choices: Wait until the next scheduled home visit to mention it
Try to figure out the cause by reviewing the client's medications
Report the change to the supervising nurse immediately
Reassure the client and document it in their personal notes
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: A client's family member asks the HHA to perform a task not listed in the care plan, such as driving the client to a doctor's appointment. The HHA should:
choices: Do it — the family's needs are part of the job
Refuse politely and explain that tasks must be authorized in the care plan
Charge the family extra for the additional service
Do it just this once to maintain a good relationship
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: When should an HHA perform hand hygiene in a client's home?
choices: Only before preparing meals
Before and after each client contact, after touching body fluids, and before leaving
Only when hands are visibly soiled
Once at the start and once at the end of each visit

hha.q: An HHA is caring for a client with a cold and runny nose. To protect themselves, the HHA should:
choices: Cancel the visit and reschedule for a different week
Wear gloves, practice diligent hand hygiene, and consider a mask if in close contact
Wear only gloves — other PPE is not necessary for a cold
Ask the client to wear a mask while the HHA is present

hha.q: When handling soiled linens in a client's home, the HHA should:
choices: Shake the linens to remove debris before placing in the laundry
Carry linens close to the body to maintain control
Hold linens away from the body, avoid shaking, and place directly in a laundry bag
Leave soiled linens on the floor until the end of the visit

hha.q: When assisting a client with a one-sided weakness (hemiplegia) to dress, the HHA should:
choices: Dress the strong side first to build confidence
Dress the weak (affected) side first
Let the client dress themselves completely without any help
Dress the client from head to toe without stopping

hha.q: A client with diabetes has thick, ingrown toenails. The HHA should:
choices: Trim the toenails carefully with nail clippers
Soak the feet and file the nails smooth
Report the condition to the nurse — foot care for diabetics is a specialized procedure
Apply a corn-removal product available at the pharmacy

hha.q: While assisting a client with a shower, the water temperature should be checked:
choices: By the client only — they know their own comfort level
By the HHA using a bath thermometer or inner wrist, then confirmed with the client
Only if the client has diabetes or circulation problems
After the client has entered the shower

hha.q: An HHA arrives at a client's home and smells gas strongly throughout the apartment. The FIRST action should be:
choices: Check the stove and open the windows before calling anyone
Turn on lights to see better
Get the client out of the home immediately and call 911 from outside
Turn off the gas at the main valve under the stove

hha.q: To reduce a client's fall risk in the home, the HHA should:
choices: Keep all furniture in the same place so the client memorizes the layout
Remove loose rugs, ensure adequate lighting, and keep pathways clear
Restrict the client to one room to minimize walking
Ask the client to call for help every time they want to move

hha.q: A client asks the HHA to help them take an extra dose of their pain medication because they are in more pain than usual. The HHA should:
choices: Give the extra dose — pain relief is a basic human need
Refuse the extra dose and report the increased pain to the supervising nurse
Give half the extra dose as a compromise
Tell the client to take it themselves so the HHA is not responsible

hha.q: A client has been prescribed a low-sodium diet. When preparing lunch, the HHA should:
choices: Add a small amount of salt since the diet allows 'low' sodium — not 'no' sodium
Follow the prescribed diet and avoid adding salt or high-sodium foods
Ask the client if they want salt — it is their home and their choice
Substitute salt with a salt substitute without checking with the nurse
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: When storing leftover food in a client's home, the HHA should:
choices: Leave food on the counter covered with a cloth — refrigeration changes flavor
Label and refrigerate leftovers promptly; discard food that has been at room temperature for 2+ hours
Refrigerate only meat — other foods are safe at room temperature
Follow whatever storage practice the client prefers
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: A client with dysphagia is prescribed nectar-thick liquids. The HHA pours the client a glass of regular water. This is:
choices: Acceptable — water is always safe to drink
A violation of the care plan that puts the client at risk for aspiration pneumonia
Acceptable if the client asks for it specifically
Only a problem if the client has a visible cough
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: A client tells the HHA, 'I don't want you to tell my children about my health — that's private.' The HHA should:
choices: Tell the family anyway — family needs to know for the client's safety
Respect the client's privacy; only share health information with those authorized to receive it
Ask the supervising nurse to tell the family instead
Agree, but write the information in their personal notes to share later
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: An HHA notices that a client's adult daughter regularly takes money from the client's wallet without the client's knowledge. This is MOST likely:
choices: Normal family financial management — not a concern
Financial exploitation / financial abuse — must be reported
Only a problem if the client complains about it
Acceptable since family members have legal authority over finances
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: A client tells an HHA, 'I want to die in my own home — I do not want to go to the hospital or have CPR.' The HHA should:
choices: Ignore this statement — the client may not be thinking clearly
Acknowledge the client's wishes and report them to the supervising nurse to ensure proper documentation (advance directive/DNR)
Call 911 the moment the client appears seriously ill regardless of their wishes
Make the decision based on the circumstances when the time comes
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: While preparing lunch, an HHA's client suddenly collapses and is unresponsive. After calling 911, the HHA should:
choices: Wait near the client for emergency services to arrive without touching the client
Check if the client has a pulse and is breathing; begin CPR if no pulse and no normal breathing
Position the client on their side and wait for 911
Call the agency first for instructions before doing anything

hha.q: A client with diabetes is sweating, shaking, confused, and says they feel dizzy. Blood glucose readings are unavailable. The HHA should suspect:
choices: Stroke — call 911 immediately without doing anything else
Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) — give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrates if the client is conscious
Hyperglycemia (high blood sugar) — withhold all food and call the nurse
A panic attack — have the client breathe into a paper bag

hha.q: An HHA finds a client on the floor. The client is awake and says their hip is very painful. The HHA should:
choices: Help the client up slowly and into a chair to assess the damage
Leave the client on the floor, keep them still and warm, and call for help immediately
Have the client try walking to see if the hip can bear weight
Apply ice and wait 30 minutes before calling anyone

hha.q: When completing a daily log for a client, the HHA should document:
choices: Only problems and emergencies — routine care doesn't need documentation
All care provided, client's condition, intake and output, and any observations
A brief note confirming the visit happened and nothing unusual occurred
Only what the supervising nurse asks them to record
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: An HHA makes an error in the daily documentation — they wrote the wrong time for a medication observation. The correct action is to:
choices: Use white-out to cover the error and write the correct information over it
Black out the error completely so it cannot be read
Draw a single line through the error, write the correct information, and initial it
Tear out the page and start over on a fresh sheet
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: An HHA is helping a client use a walker. The client should carry the walker by:
choices: Picking it up completely with each step to move forward
Sliding it along the floor to maintain continuous contact
Moving the walker forward first, then stepping into it — one side at a time
Letting the client choose whichever method they prefer

hha.q: After completing morning care, the HHA leaves a client sitting in a chair. Before leaving the room, the HHA should ensure:
choices: The TV is on so the client is entertained
The client has their phone or call device within reach and is positioned safely
The curtains are open for natural light
The client has a magazine to read

hha.q: A client with dementia becomes upset and repeatedly asks to go home, despite being in their own home. The BEST response by the HHA is:
choices: 'You ARE home — stop saying that.'
Acknowledge the feeling and redirect gently: 'You seem worried — let's have some tea together.'
Show the client their family photos to prove they are home
Tell the client they cannot leave until the HHA's shift is over
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: A client tells the HHA, 'I've been thinking about ending my life. I just don't see the point anymore.' The HHA should:
choices: Tell the client that things will get better and change the subject
Promise not to tell anyone so the client continues to feel safe sharing
Take the statement seriously, stay with the client, and report immediately to the supervising nurse
Suggest the client call their family when they feel ready
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: An HHA should avoid accepting gifts or money from clients because:
choices: It creates a conflict of interest and may violate agency policy and professional ethics
Gifts are only a problem if they are worth more than $50
It is acceptable for small gifts like food or flowers
Only the supervising nurse is allowed to accept gifts
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: An HHA who must be absent for a scheduled visit should:
choices: Ask a neighbor to check on the client
Skip the visit and make up the time on a later visit
Notify the agency as soon as possible so coverage can be arranged
Ask a friend or family member to cover the visit
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: An HHA has been caring for a terminally ill client for six months and has become emotionally attached. The client dies. The MOST appropriate way for the HHA to respond professionally is:
choices: Avoid all contact with the family after the death — it is no longer the HHA's role
Attend the funeral only if invited by the family
Acknowledge their own grief, seek support from their agency, and allow themselves to grieve appropriately
Move on immediately — professional caregivers are trained not to feel loss
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: What does 'HHA' stand for?
choices: Hospital Health Assistant
Home Health Aide
Healthcare Hygiene Associate
High-risk Health Agency
hha.exp: HHA = Home Health Aide. An HHA provides personal care and basic health services to clients in their own homes under supervision of a nurse or therapist.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: What does 'scope of practice' mean for an HHA?
choices: The size of the home they can work in
The specific tasks an HHA is legally allowed to perform
The geographic area they can work
The number of clients they can have
hha.exp: Scope of practice = the legal boundaries of what you are trained and licensed to do. HHAs provide personal care but do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or diagnose.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: Who creates and modifies the home care plan for an HHA's client?
choices: The HHA, based on daily observations
The client's family
The supervising nurse or therapist
The insurance company
hha.exp: The care plan is created by the supervising nurse or therapist. The HHA follows it exactly and reports any needed changes — never modifying it independently.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: What should an HHA do FIRST upon arriving at a new client's home?
choices: Begin cleaning immediately
Orient themselves to the emergency exits and phone
Ask the client what they want for lunch
Check the client's refrigerator for expired food
hha.exp: Safety first: know how to exit and call for help before providing care. Locate emergency exits, identify the nearest phone or confirm cell service.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: An HHA is changing a client's wound dressing at home. This task is:
choices: Within the HHA's scope of practice with proper training
Outside the HHA's scope — sterile wound care requires a nurse
Acceptable if the client or family requests it
Fine if the wound is small
hha.exp: Sterile wound care and dressing changes require a nurse. HHAs do not perform sterile procedures. The HHA should notify the supervising nurse.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: An HHA enters the client's kitchen and smells gas. The FIRST action is:
choices: Turn on the stove to check if it is the source
Open all windows and doors, and call 911 from outside
Light a match to see if there is a leak
Turn on the kitchen fan
hha.exp: Gas leaks are explosive. Do NOT create any spark (switches, matches, fans). Exit immediately, leave doors open, call 911 from outside.

hha.q: A client on a low-sodium diet asks the HHA to add extra salt to their food. The HHA should:
choices: Add the salt — the client has the right to eat what they want
Follow the dietary order and explain why salt is restricted for the client's health
Add a small amount so the client is happy
Call the doctor for permission before cooking
hha.exp: The HHA follows the care plan dietary orders. Explain the restriction kindly, use salt alternatives if approved, and report the request to the nurse.
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: An HHA notices the client appears more confused than usual and is not eating. The BEST action is:
choices: Note it and report at the next scheduled home visit
Call the supervising nurse to report the change in condition
Try different foods until the client eats
Wait to see if it improves by tomorrow
hha.exp: A change in condition (new confusion, not eating) is a reportable event — do not wait. The supervising nurse must be notified promptly.
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: A client refuses to take a bath. The HHA should:
choices: Force the bath since hygiene is part of the care plan
Respect the refusal, try to understand the reason, offer alternatives (partial bath, etc.), and document and report
Give up and never attempt personal care again
Tell the family to force the client to bathe
hha.exp: Clients have the right to refuse care. An HHA never forces care. Try alternatives, respect the right, document, and report to the nurse.
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: A client's neighbor calls asking for information about the client's health condition. The HHA should:
choices: Share basic information since the neighbor is being friendly
Refuse to share any client information — HIPAA protects client privacy
Ask the client if it is okay to share
Refer the neighbor to the client directly and share nothing
hha.exp: HIPAA applies in the home. The HHA does not share client health information with anyone — neighbors, distant relatives, or friends — without proper authorization.
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: An HHA's client tells her: 'I don't want to live anymore. I feel like a burden to everyone.' The BEST response is:
choices: 'Don't say that! Things will get better.'
'I understand you're feeling very down. I want to make sure you're safe — I'm going to call your nurse right now.'
'Let me distract you — let's watch TV together.'
'You should talk to your family about this, not me.'
hha.exp: Statements about not wanting to live must be taken seriously. Do not dismiss, deflect, or delay — report to the supervising nurse immediately. This is a potential safety crisis.
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: An HHA discovers the client has chickenpox and the HHA has never had chickenpox or been vaccinated. The HHA should:
choices: Continue providing care while wearing a regular surgical mask
Contact the supervising nurse or agency before continuing care — possible airborne exposure risk
Wear gloves and a gown and continue normally
Refuse care without notification
hha.exp: Chickenpox requires airborne precautions. An unvaccinated/non-immune HHA faces a real infection risk. The supervising nurse must determine the appropriate action.

hha.q: The client's daughter asks the HHA to give her mother an extra blood pressure pill 'just this once' because the mother forgot her morning dose. The HHA should:
choices: Give the pill — it's just one dose and the daughter is family
Decline and call the supervising nurse to report the missed dose and request guidance
Give the pill but document it
Ask the client if she wants the extra pill
hha.exp: Medication administration is outside all HHA scope of practice regardless of who asks. The nurse determines how to handle a missed dose. Do not give medications.

hha.q: An HHA visits a client's home and notices the client has bruises on her arms in various stages of healing. The client seems afraid and says 'I fell.' The BEST action is:
choices: Accept the explanation and document 'client states she fell'
Report concerns about possible abuse to the supervising nurse immediately — HHAs are mandatory reporters
Ask the client directly: 'Is someone hitting you?'
Contact Adult Protective Services independently without notifying the supervisor first
hha.exp: Multiple bruises in various stages = possible abuse pattern. HHAs are mandatory reporters. Report to the supervisor who will engage the proper channels (APS, case management).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: At the end of a home visit, an HHA realizes she forgot to document the client's vital signs she took earlier. She should:
choices: Add them to yesterday's note since it is close enough
Document them now with the correct time they were taken and a late-entry note ('late entry — omitted from earlier documentation')
Fabricate approximate numbers
Ask the client to confirm the numbers from memory
hha.exp: Late entry documentation is acceptable and legal — clearly label it. Never falsify, alter, or fabricate documentation. Accurate records protect the client and the HHA.
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: An HHA is asked by the client to be listed as a beneficiary in the client's will. The HHA should:
choices: Accept — the client can choose whoever they want
Decline and report to the supervising nurse — accepting gifts or inheritance from clients is a form of financial exploitation
Accept only if the amount is small
Ask the client to wait until after the care relationship ends
hha.exp: HHAs accepting money, gifts, or inheritance from clients is financial exploitation — a form of abuse and grounds for termination and criminal charges.
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: An HHA arrives at a client's home to find the client unresponsive on the floor and not breathing. There is no DNR on file. The HHA should:
choices: Call the supervising nurse and wait for instructions
Call 911 immediately and begin CPR if trained
Leave to find a phone since cell service is unreliable
Check the care plan before doing anything
hha.exp: No DNR = CPR is indicated. Call 911 first (dispatchers can guide CPR). Start CPR if trained. In a home setting, 911 is always the first call for a life-threatening emergency.

hha.q: An HHA disagrees with a client's lifestyle choices (diet, smoking, religious practices). The BEST approach is:
choices: Gently educate the client about healthier choices during every visit
Refuse to provide care in areas related to behaviors she disapproves of
Respect the client's autonomy and personal choices while providing professional care without judgment
Report the lifestyle choices to the supervising nurse as a health risk
hha.exp: Client autonomy = the right to make their own choices about their own life. HHAs provide non-judgmental care regardless of personal beliefs about the client's choices.
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: What does “Scope of Practice” mean?
choices: A wide belt placed around a resident's waist to provide a safe handhold during transfers and ambulation assistance.
When skin turns white (pales) briefly when pressed with a finger — a sign of normal blood flow. Non-blanching redness is an early sign of pressure ulcer.
The specific tasks an HHA/CNA is legally permitted to perform. CNAs and HHAs do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or take telephone orders.
A legal obligation for healthcare workers to report suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of vulnerable adults or children to authorities.
hha.exp: Scope of Practice: The specific tasks an HHA/CNA is legally permitted to perform. CNAs and HHAs do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or take telephone orders.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: What does “Scope of Practice” mean?
choices: The full movement possible at a joint. ROM exercises maintain flexibility and prevent contractures. Active ROM: patient moves on their own. Passive ROM: CNA moves the li…
A flexible tube inserted into the bladder to drain urine. An indwelling (Foley) catheter remains in place; requires regular care to prevent infection.
A drop in blood pressure that occurs when a person stands up suddenly, causing dizziness or fainting. Also called orthostatic hypotension.
The specific tasks an HHA/CNA is legally permitted to perform. CNAs and HHAs do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or take telephone orders.
hha.exp: Scope of Practice: The specific tasks an HHA/CNA is legally permitted to perform. CNAs and HHAs do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or take telephone orders.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: What does “Scope of Practice” mean?
choices: Failure to provide adequate care — food, fluids, hygiene, safety, or medical needs. Also reportable.
The specific tasks an HHA/CNA is legally permitted to perform. CNAs and HHAs do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or take telephone orders.
Specialized clothing or equipment worn by healthcare workers to protect against infection: gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, face shield.
Abnormally low blood pressure, generally below 90/60 mmHg. Can cause dizziness, fainting, or shock.
hha.exp: Scope of Practice: The specific tasks an HHA/CNA is legally permitted to perform. CNAs and HHAs do NOT administer medications, perform sterile procedures, or take telephone orders.
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: What does “Care Plan” mean?
choices: The correct use of the body to prevent injury during lifting, moving, and transferring patients. Key principles: wide base of support, bend at knees, keep load close to…
A written document created by the care team outlining a client's specific needs, goals, and interventions. The HHA follows the care plan; they do NOT create or modify it.
A person clutching their throat with both hands — the recognized signal of airway obstruction/choking.
A flexible tube inserted into the bladder to drain urine. An indwelling (Foley) catheter remains in place; requires regular care to prevent infection.

hha.q: What does “Dysphagia” mean?
choices: The entry of food, liquid, saliva, or vomit into the lungs instead of the stomach — can cause aspiration pneumonia.
Difficulty swallowing. Requires modified diet textures and thickened liquids to prevent aspiration.
Nil per os (Latin) — nothing by mouth. Patient must not eat or drink anything, usually before surgery or diagnostic tests.
A condition in which the body loses more fluid than it takes in. Signs: dry mouth, concentrated (dark) urine, skin tenting, confusion, dizziness.
hha.exp: Dysphagia: Difficulty swallowing. Requires modified diet textures and thickened liquids to prevent aspiration.

Measurement and recording of all fluid taken in (oral fluids, IV, tube feeds) and all fluid excreted (urine, emesis, drainage). Used to detect dehydration or fluid overl…
Fluids modified to a specific consistency (nectar-thick or honey-thick) to reduce aspiration risk for residents with dysphagia.
The entry of food, liquid, saliva, or vomit into the lungs instead of the stomach — can cause aspiration pneumonia.

A legal document stating a patient's healthcare wishes if they become unable to communicate: includes Living Will and Healthcare Proxy (DPOA-HC).
hha.exp: Abuse: Intentional harm or mistreatment of a resident — physical, emotional, sexual, or financial. CNAs are MANDATORY REPORTERS and must report all suspected abuse immediately.

hha.q: What does “Dementia” mean?
choices: A technique that gently reminds a confused resident of the current time, place, and situation to reduce disorientation.
A communication approach for dementia patients that acknowledges and respects their feelings rather than correcting their confusion.
A group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities severely enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's is the most common cause.
Increased confusion, agitation, and behavioral changes in dementia patients that worsen in the late afternoon and evening.
hha.exp: Dementia: A group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities severely enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's is the most common cause.
hha.section: 03 · Module III — Working with the Elderly

hha.q: Which term means: “A group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities severely enough to interfere with daily life. Alzh…”?
choices: Reality Orientation
Validation Therapy
Dementia
Sundowning
hha.exp: Dementia: A group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities severely enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's is the most common cause.
hha.section: 03 · Module III — Working with the Elderly

hha.q: What does “Airborne Precautions” mean?
choices: Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and negative-pressure room.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — a dangerous antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Requires contact precautions (gown + gloves).
A hospital-acquired infection — an infection a patient develops while receiving care that was not present on admission.
Specialized clothing or equipment worn by healthcare workers to protect against infection: gloves, gown, mask, eye protection, face shield.
hha.exp: Airborne Precautions: Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and negative-pressure room.

hha.q: Which term means: “Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and nega…”?
choices: Contact Precautions
Airborne Precautions
MRSA
Nosocomial Infection
hha.exp: Airborne Precautions: Used for infections spread by tiny airborne particles (e.g., TB, measles, chickenpox). Requires N95 respirator and negative-pressure room.

hha.q: What does “Vital Signs” mean?
choices: A drop in blood pressure that occurs when a person stands up suddenly, causing dizziness or fainting. Also called orthostatic hypotension.
The four primary measurements of body function: Temperature (T), Pulse (P), Respiration (R), Blood Pressure (BP). SpO₂ is often called the 5th vital sign.
High blood pressure — a reading consistently at or above 130/80 mmHg. A leading risk factor for stroke and heart disease.
Abnormally low blood pressure, generally below 90/60 mmHg. Can cause dizziness, fainting, or shock.
hha.exp: Vital Signs: The four primary measurements of body function: Temperature (T), Pulse (P), Respiration (R), Blood Pressure (BP). SpO₂ is often called the 5th vital sign.

hha.q: Which term means: “The four primary measurements of body function: Temperature (T), Pulse (P), Respiration (R), Blood Pressure (BP). SpO₂…”?
choices: Postural Hypotension
Vital Signs
Apical Pulse
Tachycardia
hha.exp: Vital Signs: The four primary measurements of body function: Temperature (T), Pulse (P), Respiration (R), Blood Pressure (BP). SpO₂ is often called the 5th vital sign.

hha.q: According to the NYS Home Care Curriculum, what is one main goal of home care?
choices: To replace the hospital for every type of medical treatment
To keep people who need support at home and out of institutions, so families can stay together
To give the family a break from all responsibility
To provide care only to children in foster care
hha.exp: Home care keeps people who need support out of hospitals, nursing homes and institutions, allows families to remain intact, and encourages independence, dignity and comfort at home (Module I, Unit A).
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: In which decade did Medicaid and Medicare begin paying for coordinated home care services?
choices: The 1930s
The 1960s
The 1980s
The 2000s
hha.exp: Training for homemakers began in the 1930s, but Medicaid/Medicare payment for coordinated home care services started in the 1960s (Module I, Unit A, History of home care).
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: The curriculum describes two categories of home care clients. Which pair is correct?
choices: Rich clients and poor clients
Persons with a specific injury or illness, and persons in need of support in the home
Children and adults
Clients with insurance and clients without insurance
hha.exp: The two categories are: a person with a specific injury/illness, and persons in need of support in the home. Clients include the frail elderly, the acutely and chronically ill, the physically and mentally challenged, and adults and children in need of protection (Module I, Unit A).
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: Which of the following is listed by the curriculum as a reason a home care worker could be dismissed?
choices: Asking the supervisor too many questions
Being disrespectful of the privacy of others
Arriving five minutes early
Refusing to give a client medication
hha.exp: Reasons for dismissal: unreliability, untrustworthiness, being disrespectful of the privacy of others, and non-compliance with agency protocols (Module I, Unit B).
hha.topic: Qualities of the Home Care Worker
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care
hha.chapter: Qualities of the Home Care Worker

hha.q: The curriculum says success as a home care worker depends on the ability to:
choices: Work without constant supervision, get along with clients, organize time, and be observant of the client's needs
Finish all tasks as fast as possible and leave early
Make medical decisions when the nurse is not available
Do exactly what the family says, even if it is not in the care plan
hha.exp: Success depends on working without constant supervision, getting along well with clients, organizing time to complete all tasks, and being observant and sensitive to the client's physical, social, spiritual and cultural needs (Module I, Unit B).
hha.topic: Qualities of the Home Care Worker
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care
hha.chapter: Qualities of the Home Care Worker

hha.q: Who coordinates the development of the client's care plan?
choices: The home care worker
The client's neighbor
The case manager, with the plan developed by the team
The pharmacist
hha.exp: The care plan is developed by the team and coordinated by the case manager. It lists duties, goals and special observations, and a copy is kept in the client's home (Module I, Unit C).
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: Which of the following is a responsibility of the RN supervisor toward the home care worker?
choices: Doing the worker's housekeeping tasks when the worker is behind
Visiting the client's home to ensure follow-up and reviewing all procedures with the worker
Paying the client's bills
Deciding which clients the worker may share information with
hha.exp: The RN supervisor visits the client's home, ensures the worker understands the care plan, reviews procedures, provides instruction, solves problems, links the worker with the team and agency, and evaluates performance (Module I, Unit C).
hha.section: 01 · Module I — Introduction to Home Care

hha.q: According to the theory of basic human needs taught in the curriculum, which needs must be met FIRST?
choices: Self-fulfillment needs
Belonging needs
Physical safety and security needs
Self-worth needs
hha.exp: Physical, safety and security needs come first; higher needs (belonging, self-worth, self-fulfillment) come next. Unmet needs create stress and change behavior (Module II, Unit A).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: A normally calm client becomes irritable and refuses to eat after her daughter stops visiting. According to the curriculum, this behavior is BEST understood as:
choices: A sign the client is simply difficult
A possible reaction to an unmet need (belonging), which creates stress
Proof that the client no longer needs home care
Something to ignore because it is a family matter
hha.exp: Needs motivate behavior and feelings. Unmet needs can create stress and clients may respond with changed behavior. The worker should recognize the unmet need and observe, record and report (Module II, Unit A).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: A client from a different culture refuses a certain food and prefers to be greeted in a specific way. The curriculum teaches that the home care worker should:
choices: Correct the client's habits to match American customs
Respect the diversity of culture, religion, food choices and communication styles, because these affect caregiving
Report the client's habits as a safety concern
Prepare the food anyway because nutrition is more important
hha.exp: Diversity (race, religion, national origin, age, sexual orientation) affects caregiving through verbal/non-verbal communication, health beliefs, food choices and family systems. The worker respects each client's individuality (Module II, Unit B).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: Which of the following is an example of NON-VERBAL communication?
choices: Explaining the bath procedure out loud
Writing a note in the log
Facial expression, posture and touch
Reading the care plan to the client
hha.exp: Communication is verbal and non-verbal. Non-verbal includes facial expression, gestures, posture, tone and touch. Effective communication also requires feedback and active listening (Module II, Unit C).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: A client has aphasia after a stroke and struggles to find words. The BEST communication approach is:
choices: Finish the client's sentences quickly so care is not delayed
Speak louder, because aphasia is a hearing problem
Be patient, use simple sentences, allow time to respond, and use gestures or pictures
Avoid talking to the client because it frustrates them
hha.exp: The curriculum requires communication techniques for special needs: vision, hearing, aphasia and cognitive impairment. Aphasia is a language problem, not a hearing problem; patience, simple language, time and visual aids help (Module II, Unit C).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: The curriculum defines a therapeutic relationship as one that is:
choices: Planned, purposeful and built on trust
Casual and based on friendship
Controlled completely by the worker
Based on the worker doing everything for the client
hha.exp: A therapeutic relationship is planned, purposeful and built on trust. It respects the client's autonomy and fosters independence rather than dependency (Module II, Unit C, Lesson 4).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: Which set of individual rights does the curriculum say every care recipient has?
choices: Free housing, free food and free transport
Autonomy, privacy, confidentiality, and freedom from abuse, neglect and mistreatment
The right to choose the worker's salary
The right to change the care plan without the nurse
hha.exp: Caregivers must allow recipients to exercise their rights to autonomy, privacy, confidentiality, and freedom from abuse, neglect and mistreatment (Module II, Unit C, Lesson 5).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: Trained observation uses which senses, according to the curriculum?
choices: Sight only
Sight, smell, hearing and touch
Taste and intuition
Only what the client tells you
hha.exp: Trained observation uses sight, smell, hearing and touch, and requires knowing what is normal for the client so changes can be detected (Module II, Unit D).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: Which note follows the curriculum's recording rules ('write only what you see, hear and do; date it; sign it')?
choices: 'Client was lazy and did not want to get up.' (no date)
'10/16 — Client stated "my chest hurts" at 9:15 AM; skin pale and sweaty; called supervisor at 9:17. — M. Diop'
'I think the client is depressed because of her son.'
'Everything fine today.'
hha.exp: Record facts: what you see, hear and do, with date and signature. Avoid opinions and judgments. Factual, dated, signed notes help the team know the client's status and protect the worker (Module II, Unit D).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: Besides changes in the client's condition, what else does the curriculum say the home care worker should observe and report?
choices: Only the client's vital signs
Environmental conditions affecting the client, and changes in supportive relationships with relatives or friends
The neighbors' activities
The worker's own feelings about the family
hha.exp: The worker observes and reports: changes in the client's condition, environmental conditions and changes that affect the client, and changes in supportive relationships with relatives/friends (Module II, Unit D).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: Which federal rule on protecting client health information is named in the curriculum's confidentiality unit?
choices: OSHA
HIPAA
FDA
DMV
hha.exp: Unit E covers the scope of confidentiality (conversations, observations, reporting), the worker's role in maintaining it, and HIPAA guidelines and compliance (Module II, Unit E).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: On the bus home, a home care worker tells a coworker funny details about a client's bathroom habits without naming the client. According to the curriculum this is:
choices: Acceptable because no name was used
A breach of confidentiality — conversations about clients, including observations, are covered
Acceptable because coworkers are part of the team
Only a problem if the client finds out
hha.exp: Confidentiality covers conversations, observations and reporting. Workers must maintain confidentiality in their personal conduct, including conversations with co-workers and others (Module II, Unit E).
hha.section: 02 · Module II — Working Effectively with Clients

hha.q: The curriculum describes aging as:
choices: A disease that must be treated
A normal process with individual variations
Something that happens the same way to everyone
A reason to stop encouraging independence
hha.exp: Aging is a normal process; there are individual variations in physical and mental changes, influenced by social factors such as family, finances, culture and spirituality (Module III, Unit A).
hha.section: 03 · Module III — Working with the Elderly

hha.q: An elderly client who used to eat well now says food has no taste and eats less. Which body system change of aging does this MOST relate to, and what should the worker do?
choices: Musculoskeletal; encourage exercise
Sensory system (taste and smell decline); observe, record and report the reduced intake
Reproductive system; nothing to report
Immune system; give vitamins
hha.exp: Module III, Unit B covers aging effects on each body system, including the sensory system (reduced taste and smell), with the worker's role to know common health problems, care for the client, and report symptoms.
hha.section: 03 · Module III — Working with the Elderly

hha.q: An elderly client suddenly becomes confused over two days. She was alert last week. According to the curriculum, this is MOST likely:
choices: A permanent change that is a normal part of aging
A temporary change in mental functioning with a possible cause (illness, medication, dehydration) that must be reported
Nothing unusual; all old people are confused
A sign the client needs a nursing home immediately
hha.exp: The curriculum distinguishes temporary changes in mental functioning (with causes such as infection, medication, dehydration) from permanent changes. A sudden change must be observed, recorded and reported (Module III, Unit C).
hha.section: 03 · Module III — Working with the Elderly

hha.q: Which of the following is a healthy technique to reduce stress that the worker can encourage, according to the curriculum?
choices: Keeping worries secret
Coping mechanisms such as talking about feelings, relaxation and keeping active
Skipping meals
Isolating from family and friends
hha.exp: Module III, Unit C covers causes and effects of stress (mental and physical), coping mechanisms and techniques to reduce stress, and the duty to observe, record and report.
hha.section: 03 · Module III — Working with the Elderly

hha.q: Which of the following is a family situation in which children may need a home care worker, according to the curriculum?
choices: The parents want free babysitting on weekends
Chronic illness of a child or parent, prematurity, or an overwhelmed parent
The child needs tutoring for school
The family wants a cook
hha.exp: Situations include chronic illness of child or parent, disability, prematurity, post-trauma, inexperienced or overwhelmed parent, death or desertion of a parent, and domestic violence, abuse, neglect or substance abuse (Module IV, Unit A).

hha.q: According to the curriculum's five stages of child development, a 'toddler' is aged:
choices: Birth to 12 months
1 to 3 years
3 to 6 years
6 to 12 years
hha.exp: Infant: birth to 12 months; Toddler: 1 to 3 years; Preschool: 3 to 6 years; School age: 6 to 11 or 12 years; Adolescent: 11 to 19 years (Module IV, Unit B).

hha.q: When working with parents and families, the curriculum advises the home care worker to:
choices: Take over parenting because the parent is overwhelmed
Show respect for the family's resources, lifestyle and culture, address the caregiver's needs at the start of each visit, and model positive parenting
Criticize the parent's methods so they improve
Report the family to authorities if their culture is different
hha.exp: Key factors: understand family roles and dynamics; show respect for the family's resources, lifestyle and culture; address the caregiver's needs at the beginning of each visit; model positive parenting techniques; observe and report (Module IV, Unit D).

hha.q: According to the curriculum, which of the following is a sign of good mental health?
choices: Never feeling anxious or frustrated
Being able to adapt to change, accept disappointment, and control impulses
Avoiding all relationships
Blaming others when things go wrong
hha.exp: Mentally healthy people can adapt to change, give and accept affection, develop good relationships, control impulses, accept responsibility, accept disappointment, tolerate some anxiety and frustration, and respect themselves (Module V, Unit A).
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: Which of the following does the curriculum list as a cause of mental illness?
choices: Laziness
Physical factors such as brain injury or chemical imbalance, heredity, environment and abnormal stress
Punishment for past actions
Eating too much sugar
hha.exp: Causes: physical factors (brain injury, chemical imbalance), environmental factors, heredity and abnormal stress. Mentally ill people can recover and lead normal lives with treatment (Module V, Unit B).
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: When observing unusual behavior in a client with mental illness, the curriculum tells the worker to:
choices: Decide what caused the behavior and write the diagnosis
Describe the behavior, note when, how often and how long it occurs, and NOT draw conclusions about the cause
Ignore it unless the family complains
Argue with the client about the behavior
hha.exp: Guidelines: describe the unusual behavior (when, how often, how long), note whether it is a change in personality, whether it is extreme or harmful, and do not draw conclusions about the causes (Module V, Unit C).
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: A client with a serious mental illness suddenly becomes extremely agitated and threatens to hurt himself. The care plan requires constant supervision. The worker should:
choices: Leave to get help from a neighbor
Call 911 for the extreme behavior change, stay safe, and do not leave the client unattended
Give the client an extra dose of his psychiatric medication
Wait until the next scheduled nurse visit
hha.exp: Maintain safety: do not leave the client unattended if the plan of care requires constant supervision; observe and report non-compliance with medication; call 911 for extreme behavior changes (Module V, Unit C).
hha.section: 05 · Module V — Mental Health & Mental Illness

hha.q: How does the curriculum distinguish a developmental disability from mental illness?
choices: They are the same thing
A developmental disability is permanent and occurs before age 22; mental illness may be temporary and can occur at any age
Mental illness is permanent; developmental disability is temporary
Developmental disabilities only affect children
hha.exp: Developmental disabilities are permanent and occur before age 22 (e.g., cerebral palsy, autism, intellectual disability). Mental illness may be temporary and can occur at any time in life (Module VI, Unit A).

hha.q: Which of the following is listed by the curriculum as an ACQUIRED cause of developmental disability?
choices: Down syndrome
Lead poisoning or brain damage during delivery
Watching too much television
Poor school attendance
hha.exp: Congenital causes include chromosomal or genetic defects (Down syndrome). Acquired causes include infections during pregnancy, brain damage during delivery, alcohol/drug abuse or poor nutrition during pregnancy, premature birth and lead poisoning (Module VI, Unit A).

hha.q: Which behavior meets the curriculum's performance standards when caring for a person with a developmental disability?
choices: Talking about the person to the family while the person is in the room
Speaking with the person, including them in decisions, and encouraging them to do as much as possible for themselves
Giving commands so tasks go faster
Doing everything for the person to avoid mistakes
hha.exp: Standards: speak politely; include people in conversations (speak with them, not about them); use positive communication; explain things understandably; encourage thinking by asking rather than commanding; encourage independence; include people in decisions and offer choices; respect differences (Module VI, Unit B).

hha.q: According to the curriculum, a diagnosis of a physical disability:
choices: Tells you exactly what the person can and cannot do
Does not indicate the person's level of function; impact on activities of daily living varies
Means the person cannot live at home
Is always permanent
hha.exp: Physical disabilities may be developmental, injury-related or disease-related, temporary or permanent. The diagnosis does not indicate level of function; what matters is the impact on activities of daily living (ADLs) and instrumental ADLs (Module VII, Unit A).

hha.q: What are the home care goals for people with physical disabilities, according to the curriculum?
choices: Promoting self-care and independence, maintaining dignity and self-worth, and preserving a normal lifestyle
Keeping the person in bed to prevent injury
Doing all tasks for the person
Limiting visitors to reduce stress
hha.exp: Goals: promote self-care and independence, maintain dignity and self-worth, preserve a normal lifestyle. The worker follows the plan of care, gives emotional support, encourages independence and helps make the environment supportive (Module VII, Unit B).

hha.q: According to the curriculum, what is the main function of protein?
choices: To provide fuel for heat and energy
To build and repair body tissues
To insulate the body
To help the thyroid gland function
hha.exp: Protein builds and repairs body tissues; sources include meat, fish, eggs, milk, soy and legumes. Carbohydrates provide fuel; fat protects organs and insulates; iodine supports the thyroid (Module VIII, Unit A).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: Which mineral does the curriculum say is needed for strong bones and teeth, blood clotting and muscle contraction?
choices: Iron
Calcium
Sodium
Iodine
hha.exp: Calcium: strong bones and teeth, blood clotting, muscle contraction. Iron makes hemoglobin; potassium helps the heart; sodium balances water; iodine serves the thyroid (Module VIII, Unit A).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: Which vitamin does the curriculum credit with strengthening blood vessel walls and aiding the healing of wounds?
choices: Vitamin A
Vitamin B
Vitamin C
Vitamin D
hha.exp: Vitamin C strengthens blood vessel walls and aids healing of wounds and bones. Vitamin A helps skin and bone growth; B helps nervous and digestive systems; D builds bones and teeth; E is an antioxidant (Module VIII, Unit A).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: Besides nutrition, what must meal planning take into account, according to the curriculum?
choices: Only the cost of food
The client's food preferences and eating habits, based on culture, religion, past experience, cost and convenience
Only what the worker likes to cook
The worker's own schedule
hha.exp: Meal planning must consider food preferences and eating habits, which depend on cultural or religious background, past experience, availability and cost, and convenience, plus calorie and special nutrient needs. Involve the client in planning (Module VIII, Unit B).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: Which cooking method does the curriculum recommend to protect nutrients?
choices: Deep frying
Steaming vegetables and cooking food only until tender
Boiling vegetables for a long time
Using mostly convenience foods
hha.exp: Avoid frying; steam-cook vegetables; bake, broil or microwave; avoid convenience foods; cook food only until tender to protect nutrients; find out how the client likes food seasoned (Module VIII, Unit C).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: A client's appetite has become poor. According to the curriculum, poor appetite may signal:
choices: That the client is being stubborn
Illness or depression, dissatisfaction with food, improper mouth care, chewing problems or medications
Nothing important
That the client should skip meals
hha.exp: Be alert to a poor appetite: it may signal illness or depression, dissatisfaction with food, improper mouth care, chewing problems, or medications. Serve small attractive portions and allow seconds (Module VIII, Unit C).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: According to the curriculum, the refrigerator should be kept at what temperature?
choices: 36°F to 40°F
50°F to 55°F
Room temperature
hha.exp: Refrigerator at 36–40°F; freezer at 0°F. Cover and date refrigerated food; use frozen foods within six months; never thaw on the counter; keep hot foods above 140°F and cold foods below 40°F (Module VIII, Unit D).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: Which of the following is a safe food handling rule from the curriculum?
choices: Taste and stir the food with the same spoon
Use cans with bulging ends if they are not expired
Never use cracked eggs and never undercook eggs
Refreeze thawed food to save money
hha.exp: Rules: wash hands before handling food; wear gloves if you have a cut; never taste and stir with the same spoon; do not use damaged cans with bulging ends; never use cracked or undercooked eggs; do not refreeze food; use cooked leftovers within 3–4 days (Module VIII, Unit D).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: When shopping with the client's money, the curriculum requires the worker to:
choices: Keep the change as a tip
Follow agency policy, save all receipts, and account for all money spent as soon as possible
Round the amounts in the log
Only report large purchases
hha.exp: Food money procedures: follow the agency's policy and procedures, save all receipts, and account for all money spent as soon as possible after shopping (Module VIII, Unit D; also Module IX).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: How does the curriculum define a 'modified diet'?
choices: Any diet the client chooses
A one-nutrient change ordered by the doctor, a change in calories, or a mechanically altered texture
A diet with no salt and no sugar
A diet the worker designs
hha.exp: Modified diet: one nutrient change in a client's diet ordered by the doctor, a change in the amount of calories, or a mechanically altered diet. 'High' means increase a nutrient; 'low' means decrease or cut it out (Module VIII, Unit E).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: A client is on a bland diet. Which foods does the curriculum say to eliminate?
choices: Rice and potatoes
Pepper, spices, alcohol and caffeine
Milk and yogurt
Bread and pasta
hha.exp: A bland diet eliminates foods assumed to irritate the gastric mucosa, such as pepper, spices, alcohol and caffeine (Module VIII, Unit E).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: When preparing a pureed meal for a client with swallowing difficulty, which practice does the curriculum require?
choices: Combine all foods together before pureeing to save time
Puree each food separately, identify each food for the client, allow time to swallow each bite, and offer extra liquids
Serve everything at room temperature
Skip seasonings because they are unsafe
hha.exp: Process tips: do NOT combine foods before pureeing; add fluid and seasonings as instructed; identify each food for the client; allow enough time to swallow each bite; offer extra liquids to prevent constipation and dehydration; use blenderized food immediately or freeze it (Module VIII, Unit E).
hha.section: 08 · Module VIII — Food, Nutrition & Meal Preparation

hha.q: According to the curriculum, when may the home care worker handle a client's money for errands?
choices: Whenever the client asks
Only as outlined in the plan of care, with accurate record keeping
Never under any circumstances
Only for amounts under twenty dollars
hha.exp: The worker may assist with shopping, buying and banking as outlined in the plan of care, and must keep accurate records of expenditures when handling the client's money (Module IX, Unit A).

hha.q: Which shopping practice does the curriculum recommend to make the most of the family's finances?
choices: Always buying brand names
Comparing prices and products, considering generic brands and buying in quantity when sensible
Shopping without a list
Buying convenience foods
hha.exp: Ways to make effective use of finances: look for bargains, compare prices and products (generic brands), buy in quantities, and apply this to food, household supplies, medicine and clothes (Module IX, Unit B).

hha.q: Why does the curriculum say a clean home matters for a home care client?
choices: It impresses the supervisor
It controls infection, reduces accidents, and meets basic needs such as comfort and self-esteem
It is the only task that matters
It allows the worker to leave early
hha.exp: A clean home: infection control (bacteria, fungus), safety and security (fewer accidents), and basic needs met (comfort, belonging, pride, self-esteem, self-fulfillment) (Module X, Unit A).
hha.section: 10 · Module X — Care of the Home

hha.q: How does housekeeping in a client's home differ from housekeeping in your own home, according to the curriculum?
choices: It does not differ
You must respect the client's customs, religion, belongings, habits and equipment, and promote the client's independence
You can rearrange furniture as you like
You decide what gets thrown away
hha.exp: Differences: respect the client's customs, religion and personal belongings; respect their housekeeping habits, equipment and supplies; homes and supplies differ; be sensitive to the client's limitations; meet basic needs; promote independence (Module X, Unit B).
hha.section: 10 · Module X — Care of the Home

hha.q: Which housekeeping practice follows the curriculum's infection control principles?
choices: Use the same cloth for the kitchen and the bathroom
Keep clean and dirty areas separate, use a separate cloth for the bathroom and a disposable wipe for the toilet
Mix bleach with other cleaners for stronger cleaning
Wear the same gloves for a week
hha.exp: Infection control: wash hands before and after each task; use housekeeping gloves and clean them daily; keep clean and dirty areas separate; separate cloth for the bathroom; disposable wipe for the toilet; read directions and never mix cleaning products (Module X, Unit D).
hha.section: 10 · Module X — Care of the Home

hha.q: When doing a client's laundry, the curriculum says to:
choices: Wash everything together in hot water
Wear gloves for linens soiled with body fluids, check pockets, sort darks, whites and delicates, and ask the client what to machine-wash or air-dry
Throw away soiled clothes
Use the client's washer without asking how it works
hha.exp: Laundry: wear gloves when handling clothes or linens soiled with body fluids; check with the client about what to wash; ask how to operate the machines; check pockets; sort darks, whites and delicates; ask what should be air dried (Module X, Unit D).
hha.section: 10 · Module X — Care of the Home

hha.q: According to the curriculum, where do household injuries occur most frequently?
choices: Living room and hallway
Kitchen and bathroom
Bedroom and closet
Garage and garden
hha.exp: Most frequent home injuries are falls, burns, cuts, poisoning, choking and electrical injury; they occur most often in the kitchen and bathroom (Module XI, Unit A).

hha.q: Which factor does the curriculum list as contributing to injuries among older adults?
choices: Too much sleep
Difficulties with balance, vision problems, confusion, effects of medication and inappropriate footwear
Eating too many vegetables
Having too many visitors
hha.exp: Factors for older adults: balance difficulties, vision problems, mental confusion, hearing loss, medication effects, reduced taste and smell, cultural practice, inappropriate footwear. Other hazards: poor lighting, stairs, scatter rugs, clutter, no handrails (Module XI, Unit A).

hha.q: A fire starts in the client's kitchen. In which order does the curriculum tell the worker to act?
choices: Extinguish, then call 911, then rescue
Rescue the client and yourself; sound the Alarm (call 911); Confine the fire by closing doors; Extinguish only if minor or Evacuate
Call the supervisor first, then 911
Open all windows, then look for the extinguisher
hha.exp: In the event of fire: Rescue (get your client and yourself to safety), Alarm (call 911), Confine (close doors, block smoke), Extinguish/Evacuate (if clothing catches fire, lie down and roll; do not fight a fire unless minor). Notify the supervisor as soon as practical (Module XI, Unit B).

hha.q: Which personal safety rule does the curriculum give for workers traveling to clients' homes?
choices: Carry cash so you can pay for emergencies
Take unsafe shortcuts to save time
Have the correct address, be aware of surroundings, avoid carrying a purse or large sums, and don't change your schedule without telling the office
Keep car doors unlocked for a quick exit
hha.exp: Personal safety: correct address and directions; be aware of surroundings and avoid unsafe shortcuts; know where phones and alarm boxes are; don't carry a purse, large sums or expensive jewelry; don't alter your schedule without telling the office; keep car doors locked (Module XI, Unit B).

hha.q: In a serious medical emergency, what sequence does the curriculum teach?
choices: Call the family, then the agency
Assess the situation, assess the victim, call for help, and remember the ABCs of first aid
Move the victim to the bed first
Give water and wait
hha.exp: Serious emergencies: assess the situation, assess the victim, call for help, remember the ABCs of first aid (Airway, Breathing, Circulation). Know your agency's incident policy and whom to contact (Module XI, Unit C).

hha.q: Which group of tasks does the curriculum define as 'personal care'?
choices: Shopping, banking and paying bills
Bathing, toileting, mouth care, ambulation, dressing, grooming, eating and transferring
Cooking and cleaning only
Giving injections and changing sterile dressings
hha.exp: Personal care = tasks related to the client's body, appearance, hygiene and movement: bathing, toileting, teeth and mouth care, ambulation, dressing/grooming, eating and transferring (Module XII, Unit A).

hha.q: When washing hands with soap and water, the curriculum says to rinse with:
choices: Hands held higher than the wrists
Hands held lower than the wrists under warm running water
Cold water only
A basin of standing water
hha.exp: Procedure XII-1: wet hands under warm running water, lather well, wash all surfaces including between fingers and under nails up to above the wrist, rinse with hands lower than the wrists, dry with a clean towel, and turn off the tap with the paper towel.

hha.q: When is an alcohol-based hand cleaner an acceptable alternative to soap and water, according to the curriculum?
choices: Always; it replaces handwashing
When there is no running water and hands are not visibly soiled
Only after using the bathroom
Never
hha.exp: Alcohol-based hand cleaners are used when there is no running water or hands are not visibly soiled: apply product, rub all surfaces of hands and fingers until dry (Procedure XII-1).

hha.q: Which of the following lists the modes of transmission of infection taught in the curriculum?
choices: Direct contact, indirect contact, airborne, common vehicle and vector-borne
Only direct contact
Only airborne
Hereditary and environmental
hha.exp: Transmission: contact (direct and indirect), airborne, common vehicle (contaminated food, water, equipment) and vector-borne (insects). Risk factors: age, chronic illness, immunosuppression. Types: UTI, respiratory, wound/skin, GI (Module XII, Unit B, Infection Control).

hha.q: Which diseases does the curriculum name as bloodborne pathogens?
choices: Flu and the common cold
Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV
Chickenpox and measles
Tuberculosis and pneumonia
hha.exp: Bloodborne pathogens: hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. Vaccination (hepatitis B) is covered. Prevent exposure with safe handling of sharps, sharps containers, contaminated supplies and body fluid spills (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 3).

hha.q: What does 'Standard Precautions' mean, as taught in the curriculum?
choices: Precautions used only with clients known to be infected
Infection-control practices used with ALL clients, including handwashing, gloves/PPE, care of supplies, and safe waste and sharps disposal
Wearing a mask at all times
Refusing care to clients with infections
hha.exp: Standard (Universal) Precautions apply to all clients: the concept of clean and dirty, handwashing per CDC guidelines, care of supplies and equipment, waste and sharps disposal, and PPE/gloves (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 2).

hha.q: While cleaning up, a worker's bare skin with a small cut is splashed with a client's blood. According to the curriculum this is:
choices: Nothing to worry about if washed with water
An exposure incident; wash the area and follow the agency's exposure incident procedure and report it immediately
Only a concern if the client is known to have HIV
Something to mention at the end of the month
hha.exp: The curriculum requires knowing procedures for all exposure incidents: blood exposures, airborne exposures and latex allergy. Wash immediately, report and follow agency procedure (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 4).

hha.q: When reporting a client's pain, which characteristics does the curriculum say to include?
choices: Only whether the client is complaining
Site, duration, intensity and triggers
The worker's opinion of whether the pain is real
Only the time of day
hha.exp: Report pain by its characteristics: site (where), duration (how long), intensity (how strong) and triggers (what makes it worse). Remember cultural differences in showing pain, and that pain affects function (Module XII, Unit B, Freedom from Pain).

hha.q: A client never says he is in pain, but he grimaces, guards his side and has stopped walking to the kitchen. The curriculum teaches that the worker should:
choices: Assume there is no pain because he did not complain
Recognize non-verbal signs of pain, gather more information, and report
Give him a pain pill from the cabinet
Tell him to be brave
hha.exp: Individuals show pain in different ways, including non-verbally, and cultural background affects how pain is expressed. The worker gathers information and reports effectively (Module XII, Unit B, Freedom from Pain).

hha.q: Before placing a bedpan under a client, Procedure XII-17 says the worker should:
choices: Place it cold to make the client finish quickly
Warm and powder the bedpan, place a protector pad near the hips, and maintain privacy
Ask the family to do it
Skip handwashing because gloves are worn
hha.exp: Procedure XII-17 (Use of a Bedpan): explain, wash hands, gloves as needed, warm and powder the bedpan, place a protector pad, maintain privacy, assist the client to lift hips or roll, provide toilet paper and call signal, observe and measure contents if indicated, clean, wash hands, record and report.

hha.q: Which types of catheters does the curriculum describe?
choices: Condom, indwelling and straight catheters
Only indwelling catheters
Nasal and oral catheters
Catheters are never used at home
hha.exp: Types: condom (external), indwelling and straight catheters. The worker assists with catheter use, skin and tubing care, emptying the drainage bag and measuring output, and reports color/odor of urine, pain, chills, sweating and leakage (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 3 Incontinence).

hha.q: When emptying a urinary drainage bag (Procedure XII-21), which observation must be reported?
choices: Clear, pale yellow urine in the expected amount
Cloudy, strong-smelling or bloody urine, or little or no urine when the bag is due to be drained
That the client was asleep
That the bag was half full
hha.exp: Procedure XII-21: do not touch the end of the drainage tube; measure if directed; observe color, odor, mucus or blood; report cloudy, strong-smelling or bloody urine, and a very small or absent amount of urine when scheduled to drain.

hha.q: The curriculum lists emotional problems associated with incontinence. The worker's response should be to:
choices: Scold the client so it does not happen again
Protect dignity and privacy, change adult briefs following guidelines, and give skin care
Leave the client in wet briefs until the next scheduled change
Tell the family it is their job
hha.exp: Incontinence causes embarrassment and loss of dignity. Care includes guidelines for changing adult briefs and skin care, with observing, reporting and recording (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 3).

hha.q: What is the 'clock method' taught in the curriculum for assisting with eating?
choices: Feeding the client every hour on the hour
Describing where foods are on the plate as positions on a clock face, for a visually impaired client
Timing each bite with a stopwatch
Serving meals at exactly the same time daily
hha.exp: The clock method of tray set-up explains to a visually impaired client where each food is located on the plate (e.g., meat at 6 o'clock). Procedure XII-11 also says to feed to the strong side if there is facial weakness (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 2).

hha.q: To prevent choking at mealtime, the curriculum stresses:
choices: Feeding the client lying flat
Proper upright positioning and allowing the client to eat at their own pace
Serving only liquids
Feeding quickly so food stays hot
hha.exp: Proper positioning (sitting upright) prevents choking. Encourage the client to do as much as possible, cut food if needed, use straws or training cups, and wipe the mouth as needed (Module XII, Unit B, Lesson 2; Procedure XII-11).

hha.q: According to Procedure XII-31, what weight change should be reported?
choices: Any change of one pound
A gain or loss of more than five pounds, or client concerns about weight
Only weight gain
Weight is never reported
hha.exp: Procedure XII-31 (Weighing a Client): check the scale reads zero, support the client, note the weight when the dial stops, record it, and report a gain or loss of more than five pounds or client concerns about weight.

hha.q: Which of the following are pressure points named in the curriculum?
choices: Fingertips and nose
Coccyx, heels, sacrum, ischial tuberosities, back of the skull and elbows
Knees and chin only
Palms of the hands
hha.exp: Pressure points: coccyx, heels, sacrum, ischial tuberosities (sitting bones), back of the skull and elbows. Early signs of skin breakdown: redness, warmth, rash, itching (Module XII, Unit B, Integumentary).

hha.q: During a back rub (Procedure XII-7), the worker notices a reddened area over the client's sacrum that does not fade. The worker should:
choices: Rub the red area harder to improve circulation
Observe, record and report the reddened area to the supervisor; it may be early skin breakdown
Cover it with a bandage and say nothing
Apply heat
hha.exp: The back rub is a time to observe skin. Reddened or open areas must be reported to the supervisor. Redness, warmth, rash and itching are early signs of pressure-related skin breakdown (Module XII, Unit B, Integumentary; Procedure XII-7).
